procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated October 27, 1969, in Election Petition No. 1 of 1969, dismissing the election petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election of Respondent No. 1 to the State Legislative Assembly. The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that Respondent No. 1 was not disqualified under s. 8(2) of the Representation of the People Act and that the rejection of certain ballot papers was valid.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court under section 116-A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, challenging the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether a candidate is considered disqualified on the date of election under s. 8(2) of the Act if their conviction, existing on that date, is subsequently set aside on appeal.

facts: A candidate (respondent No. 1) was convicted and sentenced to ten years' imprisonment on January 11, 1969.
The election polling took place on February 9, 1969, and the result was declared on February 11, 1969, with the convicted candidate winning.
While the election petition challenging his victory was pending, the candidate's appeal was allowed, and his conviction was set aside (he was acquitted) on September 30, 1969.
The High Court then delivered its judgment on the election petition on October 27, 1969.
law: Under s. 8(2) of the Representation of the People Act, a person convicted of certain offenses and sentenced to imprisonment for not less than two years is disqualified from the date of the conviction.
Under s. 100(1)(a) of the Act, an election can be declared void if the High Court is of the opinion that the winning candidate was disqualified 'on the date of his election'.

The key legal principle applied by the Court is that an acquittal in a criminal appeal has a retrospective effect. It doesn't just take effect from the date of the appellate order but is considered to have wiped out the original conviction from the date it was first recorded.
application: The appellant argued that the candidate was factually disqualified on the date of the election (February 9/11, 1969) because the conviction existed on that date, and the subsequent acquittal could not change that historical fact.

The Supreme Court rejected this argument by focusing on the retrospective effect of the acquittal. It reasoned that the acquittal on September 30, 1969, completely wiped out the conviction as if it had never happened, dating back to the original trial court decision of January 11, 1969.
The Court noted that the High Court must form its opinion on the candidate's disqualification at the time it delivers its judgment on the election petition.

When the High Court made its decision on October 27, 1969, it had the acquittal order before it. Since this acquittal had retrospectively erased the conviction, it was impossible for the High Court to form the opinion that the candidate was disqualified on the election date.

The Court compared the situation to a law being retrospectively repealed. If the disqualification law itself had been repealed with effect from before the election, the candidate could not be considered disqualified. The acquittal had a similar retrospective effect, wiping out the basis for the disqualification.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the candidate was not disqualified. Because the subsequent acquittal in the criminal appeal had a retrospective effect, it completely wiped out the conviction from the date it was recorded. Therefore, when the High Court decided the election petition, it could not find that the candidate was disqualified on the date of the election.

issue.issue_text: Whether the rejection of ballot papers under rule 56(2)(b) of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, requires a definite finding that the marks were made with an instrument other than the one supplied for the purpose.

facts: An appellant challenged an election, partly on the grounds that 64 ballot papers cast in his favour were wrongly rejected by the Returning Officer.
The Returning Officer rejected them because the marks were made with an instrument other than the one supplied for voting.
The High Court reviewed the ballots and found that they bore "no recognisable seal impression that might be said to have been made with the instrument supplied for marking the vote."
The appellant argued that this finding was insufficient for rejection, as it was not a definite finding that a different instrument was used, only that the mark was unidentifiable.
law: Rule 56(2)(b) of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, states that a returning officer shall reject a ballot paper if "it bears a mark made otherwise than with the instrument supplied for the purpose."
application: The Supreme Court addressed the appellant's argument that a 'definite finding' of a different instrument being used is necessary for rejection.
The Court held that the burden was on the appellant, who was challenging the rejection, to prove that the marks were indeed made with the supplied instrument. The appellant failed to do so.
The Court reasoned that the High Court's finding—that the marks could not be identified with the official seal—was a sufficient basis for the rejection.
From this finding, the Court stated that "an inference follows that they must have been made by some other means."
Therefore, an explicit or definite finding that a different instrument was used is not required; an inference drawn from the unidentifiable nature of the mark is enough to uphold the rejection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument. It decided that a definite finding that a different instrument was used is not required for rejection under Rule 56(2)(b). A finding that the mark on the ballot is unidentifiable as having been made by the official seal is sufficient, as it gives rise to the inference that another instrument was used, especially when the challenger fails to prove otherwise.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by framing issues based on the pleadings in the written statement challenging the correctness of ballot papers without a recrimination being filed by the respondent under section 97 of the Act.

facts: The appellant argued that the High Court should not have framed issues based on the respondent's written statement, which challenged the counting of certain ballot papers.

The appellant's argument was that such challenges could only be raised through a formal 'recrimination' petition under section 97 of the Representation of the People Act, which the respondent had not filed.
law: The Supreme Court noted the legal question raised by the appellant regarding the necessity of a recrimination petition under section 97 of the Act.
application: The Supreme Court decided that it was not necessary to rule on the legal question of whether a recrimination was required.

Instead, the Court conducted a mathematical analysis of the election results based solely on the issues raised in the appellant's original election petition, completely ignoring the issues raised by the respondent that the appellant objected to.
The Court calculated the vote changes based only on the findings favorable to the appellant: the appellant gained 129 votes, and the respondent lost 98 votes.
After this recalculation, the respondent was left with 13,410 votes, while the appellant had 13,400 votes.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument because, even if the appellant was correct on the law and the issues from the respondent's written statement were ignored, the respondent still won the election with a majority of 10 votes. Therefore, deciding the legal question would not have changed the final outcome of the case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a candidate is considered disqualified on the date of election under s. 8(2) of the Act if their conviction, existing on that date, is subsequently set aside on appeal.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, implied by the issue, is that respondent No. 1 was disqualified on the date of the election (polling on Feb 9, 1969) because he had a conviction against him at that time, even though an appeal was pending. The subsequent setting aside of the conviction (on Sep 30, 1969) does not retroactively cure the disqualification that existed on the election date.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's argument, implied by the High Court's finding which was upheld, is that the subsequent acquittal in an appeal relates back to the date of the original conviction, effectively nullifying the disqualification from the outset. Therefore, he was not legally disqualified on the date of the election.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the rejection of ballot papers under rule 56(2)(b) of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, requires a definite finding that the marks were made with an instrument other than the one supplied for the purpose.
appellant_arguments: For a ballot to be rejected under rule 56(2)(b), there must be a definite finding that a different instrument was used.

The High Court's finding that the 64 ballot papers bore 'no recognisable seal impression' is insufficient for rejection, as it only means the marks *may or may not* have been made with the correct instrument.
Therefore, these 64 votes should have been counted in the appellant's favour.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct in upholding the rejection of these votes.
A finding that the marks could not be identified with the supplied seal is sufficient for rejection, as it leads to the inference that they must have been made by some other means.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by framing issues based on the pleadings in the written statement challenging the correctness of ballot papers without a recrimination being filed by the respondent under section 97 of the Act.
appellant_arguments: The High Court committed a legal error by framing three issues based on the respondent's written statement, which challenged the correctness of ballot paper counting, because the respondent had not filed a recrimination under section 97 of the Act.
respondent_arguments: No arguments from the respondent are recorded on this point, as the court chose not to decide the question of law.

statutes.act_name: The Representation of the People Act, 1951
The Representation of the People Act, 1951

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an election petition challenging the rejection of ballot papers, the burden of proof is on the petitioner to establish that the marks on the ballots were made with the instrument supplied for that purpose. A finding that the marks cannot be identified with the official seal is insufficient to discharge this burden and supports the inference that the marks were made by other means, thus justifying their rejection.
obiter: The setting aside of a conviction and sentence in an appeal has the effect of retrospectively wiping out the disqualification.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal was dismissed because none of the appellant's challenges were successful. The Court held that the respondent was not disqualified, as his subsequent acquittal on appeal retroactively nullified the conviction that existed on election day. The Court also affirmed the rejection of contested ballot papers, finding that an unidentifiable seal impression was sufficient grounds for rejection. Finally, the Court determined that even if the appellant had succeeded on a procedural point regarding the framing of issues, the respondent would still have won the election based on the final vote tally, rendering that legal question moot.
legal_tests_applied: An acquittal in a criminal appeal has the effect of retrospectively wiping out the conviction and sentence, meaning a candidate is not considered disqualified on the date of election if their conviction is later set aside.

For a ballot paper to be rejected under rule 56(2)(b) of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, a finding that the marks made could not be identified with the supplied seal is sufficient, as an inference follows that they must have been made by some other means; a definite finding that a different instrument was used is not required.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the respondent was disqualified on the date of the election failed because the court ruled that a subsequent acquittal in an appeal retrospectively wipes out the conviction, meaning the disqualification never legally existed.

The challenge to the rejection of 64 ballot papers failed because the High Court's finding that they bore 'no recognisable seal impression' was deemed sufficient to uphold their rejection, as it supported the inference that an improper instrument was used.

The procedural argument that the High Court erred by framing issues without a recrimination being filed was not decided upon, as the court found it unnecessary. Even if the appellant's position on this issue was accepted and the contested votes were ignored, the respondent still had a majority of 10 votes, making the point irrelevant to the outcome.
why_respondent_won: The respondent was found not to be disqualified because the court held that the 'setting aside of the conviction and sentence in appeal has a similar effect of wiping out retrospectively the disqualification.'

The respondent's election was upheld because the court affirmed the High Court's decision on the rejected ballot papers, stating, 'On this finding the High Court was right in not upsetting the order of Returning Officer for rejecting these votes.'

The respondent ultimately won because a final calculation of votes, even on terms most favorable to the appellant's procedural arguments, showed that 'respondent No. 1 is left with 13,410 votes, Respondent No. 1, thus, has a majority of 10 votes, so that his election is valid.'
